items.quote: Large flames increase in size over time until the flame extinguishes due to radiative heat loss.
Flame size increases with reactant flow rate and decreases with ambient oxygen concentration.
In these flames, structure has a defining influence on soot production, with soot suppressed entirely when nitrogen is supplied with the fuel.

While the flames can burn for minutes in elevated oxygen concentrations, like those being considered for future spacecraft, they were found to self-extinguish in concentrations below ~25% (by volume).
While smaller flames can burn for minutes at elevated oxygen concentrations, larger flames were generally seen to self-extinguish within 1.5 minutes.
Low-momentum microgravity flames can burn for minutes in the absence of an air flow or flame spread.
Sooty microgravity flames are taller & wider and contain 5x to 8x more soot than equivalent 1G flames.
Microgravity increases the limits of fuel dilution.
There are clear correlations between flame luminosity, combustion intensity, and ion current.
Highly-diluted flames can be stabilized with very weak electric fields.
Radiative extinction seems to occur at high flow rates and kinetic extinction at low flow rates.
With helium, rather than nitrogen, dilution of both the fuel and oxygen, the extinction limits are shifted and kinetic extinction is generally difficult to discern.
The 1g blowoff for the 1/4" rod is at 16% oxygen, whereas we obtained steady spreading at 13.6% oxygen in BASS-II.
Thus the material has a negative Oxygen Margin of Safety of 2.4% O2, and the normal gravity flammability limits should be de-rated by at least that much.

the combustion products from a fire of the scale of a BASS-II test would quickly be diluted, so that even within just the U.S. Lab (106-m3 pressurized volume), the CO levels in the lab would only be 1.5 ppm, well below spacecraft maximum allowable concentration (SMAC) values for even long-term exposure (10 ppm), let alone the 1 hour SMAC of 55 ppm (Ref. 12).
even these burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing. This has implications for spacecraft fire safety since a tiny flame might be undetected for a long time.
At the lowest speeds examined (less than 1 cms) all the flames tended to become dim blue and very stable.

Large n-alkane droplets exhibited quasi-steady low-temperature burning and extinction following radiative extinction of the visible flame while smaller droplets burned to completion or disruptively extinguished.
The ISS cabin was found to be a very clean environment with particulate levels substantially below the space shuttle and typical ground-based environments.

Despite this limiting O2 concentration for ignition, flames ignited at a higher O2 survived to final O2 concentrations as low as 13.6 percent O2, indicating that the high heat loss to the initially cold rod will quench a postignition flame while a developed solid phase temperature profile allows a sustained flame down to these low ambient O2 concentrations.
large n-alkane droplets can continue to burn quasi-steadily following radiative extinction in a low-temperature regime
The experiments also show that the limiting oxygen index for methanol in these diluent gases is around 12% to 13% oxygen by volume.
At one atmosphere pressure, ignition and some burning were observed for an oxygen concentration of 13% with the rest being nitrogen.
Observed LOI values for these fuels appear to be slightly lower than initially expected.
Average flame spread rate is 1.8 mm/s; estimated average flame power is 1200 +/- 300 W
Flame spread over a large thin charring surface in low-gravity showed that steady flame spread was possible (unlike normal gravity).
For the concurrent flame spread test, the flame size remained constrained after the ignition transient, which is not the case in 1-g.
Concurrent flame spread (with the wind) was shown to be more sensitive to the flow duct dimension than previously anticipated.

Overall the majority of the average smoke particle sizes were found to be in the 200 nm to 400 nm range with the quiescent cases producing some cases with substantially larger particles.
For the conditions tested, the materials emit most of their particulate in the submicron range.
The ISS detector showed a relatively weak signal for some Teflon runs doubtless a result of the particle size.
The zero flow conditions produced smoke particles that were 2 to 3 times larger than those produced at the nominal 8 cm/s flow rate.
all samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are readily detected using an ionization smoke detector.
